steps.say: This is a theatre in Oxford, mapped by a person walking it with a LiDAR scanner. The white line is their path.

steps.caption: Narrow stairwells: where LiDAR odometry drifts
steps.say: The hard part is the stairwells. Narrow, twisting, few flat surfaces. This is where most LiDAR odometry drifts.

scenes.headline: How Voxel-SLAM keeps a LiDAR map straight
scenes.sub: Planes, a sliding window, loops, and a run on three real walks
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Octant! Voxel-SLAM is the full mapping system from the lab behind FAST-LIO2. Here is how it works, and what it did on three real walks.

steps.say: Odometry registers each new scan against the planes in the map, with the same kind of filter FAST-LIO2 uses.
Local mapping then adjusts the last ten scans together, so a scan that went in slightly wrong can still be corrected.
Loop closure spots a place it has seen before and pulls the whole pose graph into agreement.
And when the data ends, a bundle adjustment over the whole session lines up every wall one more time.

scenes.title: Why a plane BA beats scan-to-map

labels: Window BA: scans 2 and 3 move together
The plane is solved, never stored
One cluster per scan, not every point

steps.say: Three scans of one straight wall, with the height stretched so centimetres show. Scan two was registered badly earlier, and that error is already in the map.
steps.term: Scan-to-map: one pose against fixed map planes

steps.say: Scan-to-map registration moves only the new scan. It fits the map as it stands, so it lands on a wall that is not there.
Bundle adjustment moves scans two and three together, against the anchor. Each iteration refits the plane through every point.
The plane never becomes a variable. Its normal is the eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue, and that eigenvalue is the cost.
And each scan only needs three numbers per plane: a count, a sum, and a sum of outer products. The optimiser never touches a point.
steps.term: Point cluster: a scan's points, summed

steps.say: When a loop closes, the odometry has already moved on. Some scans left the window during the solve, and ten more are still in it.
So every scan past the graph gets the last node's correction, and the local map is rebuilt from them before the odometry carries on.

scenes.title: Loop candidates on the Oxford walk

states.say: On a walk round an Oxford college quad, the place recogniser proposed forty-five loop candidates.
Twenty-nine passed the checks: a well-constrained match, and a drift under one percent of the distance walked.
states.term: Drift gate: reject loops implying over 1% drift

scenes.credit: my run, rendered by the shootout harness

steps.caption: Full SLAM, 283 m, ATE 3.20 cm
steps.say: One optimisation near the end, when the walk came back to its start, and a global bundle adjustment after it. Three point two centimetres over two hundred and eighty-three metres.

scenes.title: Error on the Oxford walk
scenes.note: ATE after one SE(3) alignment, no scale
scenes.say: Its odometry alone is six point six centimetres, a little better than FAST-LIO2's seven point two. Closing the loop halves it.

left.title: PV-LIO, same plane map
left.say: In the Sheldonian stairwells, PV-LIO, which runs the same kind of plane map under a filter, drifted one point seven three metres.

right.title: Voxel-SLAM, full SLAM
right.say: Voxel-SLAM held it to eight point two one centimetres, with no loop at all. The global bundle adjustment at the end did the rest.

scenes.label: peak memory on the Oxford walk, against 277 MB for FAST-LIO2
scenes.say: The price is memory and time. It keeps every scan for loop closure and global mapping: over four gigabytes for a five-minute walk.
